entry.dc:title: SALINE AND SODIC SPOILS - WHAT ARE THEY AND HOW ARE THEY RECLAIMED?
entry.dc:creator: Barth R.C.
entry.dc:description: Spoils classified as saline or as sodic are frequently generated by surface mining in the western United States; these have chemical properties which can be detrimental to plant growth. However, with proper management of such spoils, reclamation is possible without incurring high costs. When spoils surfaces are saline or sodic, it is suggested that expert help be obtained. Experts can make detailed recommendations suited to particular situations.

entry.dc:title: OVERVIEW OF NEW SURFACE MINING METHODS OF STEEP SLOPES IN THE APPALACHIAN REGION.
entry.dc:creator: Lusk B.
entry.dc:description: The purpose of the study is to develop a mining system that will recover a maximum amount of coal with minimum surface disturbance. Longwall stripping will also give mining companies a third alternative in situations where conventional underground or surface mining methods are not particularly adaptable.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Aiken G.
entry.dc:description: Legislation, mining engineering education, and equipment technology are discussed.

entry.dc:title: COAL RESEARCH PROJECTS IN MINING AND PREPARATION PROLIFERATE AS GOVERNMENT STEPS UP FUNDING.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: The United States' coal industry is participating in numerous projects designed to increase productivity and safety in coal mines. An overview of the leading innovations coming, many of which are federally sponsored, is presented. These include: new equipment for improving safety, speedier mining techniques, speedier coal haulage, improved surface mining methods, and new coal preparation techniques. The Bureau of Mines has been given the lead role in planning and implementing the long-range R&D program in coal extraction and preparation that would probably involve 500 million in the next five years.

entry.dc:title: KENTUCKY COAL RESERVES: EFFECTS ON COAL INDUSTRY STRUCTURE AND OUTPUT.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.prism:publicationName: Univ Ky Inst Min Miner Res Rep IMMR
entry.dc:description: The quantity and quality of land with coal reserves in a region act as the long run limit to industry output and are a primary determinant of industry structure. The present reserve base in Kentucky seems quite large relative to current output rates, and exhaustion appears to be a very distant problem. Nevertheless, the effects of the land constraint on the Kentucky coal industry structure and growth prospects over the next decade may be considerable. This report includes a survey of the conceptual links between the land factor and the coal industry. Output growth in Kentucky during the 1955-1972 period is examined from an industry structure point of view. Changes in output are described in terms of changes in average mine size and number of mines. These structural variables are also compared with the same statistics for the nation and for the states of West Virginia and Illinois. This comparative analysis yields some insight into changes in the relative ranking of Kentucky coal lands. The impact of surface mining technology on the Kentucky coal industry is stressed.

entry.dc:title: TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATIONS ABOUND IN COAL MOUNTAINS OF APPALACHIA.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: This article reviews some of the technical innovations which have been adopted by the Appalachian coal operators. Included among these are high-speed tunneling machines for coal mines, longwall shields, shortwall equipment, continous haulage systems, underground diesels, methane drainage, new surface mining techniques, and improved coal preparation equipment.

entry.dc:title: MONITORING OF ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF COAL STRIP MINING FROM SATELLITE IMAGERY.
entry.dc:creator: Brooks R.L.
entry.dc:description: A large variety of camera/film/filter combinations has been reviewed for this study. The investigation includes determining the applicability of satellite imagery for detection of disturbed acreage in areas of coal surface mining, and the much more detailed monitoring of specific surface mining operations including: active mines, inactive mines, highwalls, ramp roads, pits, water impoundments and their associated acidity, graded areas and types of grading, and reclaimed areas. Techniques have been developed to enable mining personnel to utilize this imagery in a practical and economic manner. To corroborate the photo interpretation results on-site observations were made.

entry.dc:title: Predicting the reclamation of land after surface mining in the Central Chernozem Region
entry.dc:creator: Kirillova T.B.
entry.dc:description: A methodology is proposed for forecasting the area of land likely to be disturbed by surface mining activities and the portion of the disturbed land subject to rehabilitation for various land uses (farming, woodland, ponds, outdoor recreation, built up areas, etc.). The Central Chernozem Region includes not only peat bogs, sand and clay quarries, chalk and limestone pits and phosphate mines, but also the large iron ore operations of the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, destined to become some of the leading iron ore producers of the Soviet Union. Iron ore, chalk and limestone pits and associated spoil banks now account for 20% of all disturbed land in the region, and their share is expected to grow to 40%. The total land area disturbed by surface mining in the Central Chernozem Region is expected to grow from 27,200 hectares in late 1970 to 63,000 hectares by 1990, or an increase of 2.3 times. According to the forecast, 46,400 hectares of the long term disturbance will be subject to reclamation, with 16,300 hectares for farming uses, 18,500 for woodland, 8,500 for ponds, and 3,200 for outdoor recreation, built up areas and other miscellaneous uses.

entry.dc:title: A venture into reclamation
entry.dc:creator: Balzer J.
entry.dc:description: Details on the land reclamation program carried out by Utah International Inc. at their Navaho mine near Farmington, New Mexico, are presented. The mining activities at this desert site are based on conventional surface mining methods. The earliest land reclamation efforts, which were based on ash disposal from the local power plant, are reviewed, and the result of soil surveys and cooperative studies of possible reclamation methods are discussed. The use of test plots, irrigation and other planting techniques is also considered.

entry.dc:title: COAL SURFACE MINING RECLAMATION COSTS - APPALACHIAN AND MIDWESTERN COAL SUPPLY DISTRICTS.
entry.dc:creator: Evans R.J.
entry.dc:description: Reclamation costs were estimated for 20 coal surface mining operations in the Appalachian and Midwestern Coal Supply Districts (these two districts were divided into three multi-State regions). The cost data were obtained through onsite observations, interviews with mining company personnel, and the authors' cost estimating procedures. The cost data are presented in terms of dollars per acre, dollars per ton of coal produced, and dollars per cubic yard of overburden moved during backfilling. The reclamation process is divided into three cost categories: Premining planning, backfilling, and revegetation. The average total reclamation costs for the three regions are 2. 77 per ton of coal produced and 8168 per acre. As the result of comparisons of reclamation costs by region, by mining method, by slope, and by size of operation, the most important reclamation cost difference is between area mining methods (1. 73 per ton) and contour mining methods (3. 81 per ton).

entry.dc:title: Environmental protection and beekeeping
entry.dc:creator: Engelhardt W.
entry.dc:description: The impoverishment of the West German landscape is discussed from the point of view of the beekeeper. The author reviews the increasing utilization of space for residential buildings, industrial plants and traffic facilities at the cost of agricultural and natural areas, the large scale disturbance of ecosystems and advance of monocultures, and the serious decrease of the number of different plant and animal species. Possibilities for the enrichment of landscape are mentioned, such as the recultivation of surface mining areas and reorganization of worked sand and gravel pits, the creation of new ecosystems within the framework of field clearing, and planning for the use of forests that considers not only wood production but also recreational uses and functions important to the beekeeper.

entry.dc:title: CAN SURFACE MINING BE COMPATIBLE WITH URBANIZATION?
entry.dc:creator: Coates W.E.
entry.dc:description: The compatibility or social acceptability of surface mining in and near urban areas is investigated at two points in time: (1) during the active extraction period and (2) after completion of extraction. Those features which make the typical surface mining operation quite dissimilar to normal urban uses are examined with respect to the objections usually raised by neighboring, nonextractive land owners. Means of amelioration available to the operator to mitigate the adverse impacts causing the objections are examined. Compatibility versus urbanization is investigated in terms of after-use potential. The consideration of extractive operations as ″interim″ land uses is investigated in a variety of site situations. Variations in time of after-use planning, with respect to the age of the operation and ″futuristic″ after-use potential, are investigated through case-study examples and schematic-study proposals.

entry.dc:title: FUTURE FOR PITS AND QUARRIES IN ONTARIO.
entry.dc:creator: Jewett G.
entry.dc:description: The seemingly endless array of arguments for and against the surface mining of aggregates are reduced to a relatively few key issues that are reviewed in this paper. There is no known ″elixir vitae″ for the malady. Government's role is seen as one of factilitating a free exchange of viewpoints and ideas between informed representatives of concerned agencies, followed by the development of a provincial policy that must be the framework within which individual cases will be resolved. Some of the alternatives that have been proposed are reviewed.

entry.dc:title: Hydrological impacts associated with coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Rechard P.
entry.dc:description: The extent and types of hydrologic impacts caused by the surface mining of coal are examined with regard to the influence of mine location, characteristics of the area and mining techniques used. Special attention is given to the studies carried out in the semiarid Eastern Powder River Basin of Wyoming. The possible hydrologic impacts of surface coal mining are examined with regard to the water requirements for use onsite and the impact of mining of the overall hydrologic cycle. Consideration is given to alterations in surface water runoff patterns, effects on alluvial valley floors, stream channel erosion, and creation of lakes and ponds in water short localities.

entry.dc:title: AVAILABILITY OF COAL IN ENERGY CRUNCH.
entry.dc:creator: Potter C.
entry.prism:publicationName: AAPG Bulletin American Association of Petroleum Geologists
entry.dc:description: The coal reserves in the United States are well known, both as to geologic age and geographic distribution. The largest reserves must be obtained by underground mining methods (about 327 billion tons in the east; 22 billion tons in the west), with approximately 35 billion tons obtainable from surface mining in the western United States and 10 billion tons from the eastern states. The economics of coal mining have been traditionally controlled by the quality of the coal, the cost of production, and the cost of transportation. Environmental considerations have upset the usual supply and demand pattern, and may cause further serious readjustments in mining and marketing practices.

entry.dc:title: Pseudo-Mining Subsidence through Lowering of the Water Table.
entry.dc:creator: Nendza H.
entry.dc:description: Deformation of the surface caused through lowering of the water table, such as occurring in surface mining of lignite deposits, often appear as those that are caused by mining subsidence. They are designated as pseudo-mining damages. It has been acertained by means of investigating models that deformations of the surface, overlaying a geologic fault which creates different water tables, are similar in the scope and occurence to those induced by mining.

entry.dc:title: POSEIDON STORY.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Starting with the 1969 discovery of a nickel deposit, located about 167 mi northeast of Kalgoorlie, the Poseidon Ltd has developed two mines - one underground, the other a surface mine - and put on stream on 8/28/1974 a 1-million tonnes/yr sulfides flotation concentrator. Paper describes the geologic setting of the deposit; its mineralization; and underground and surface mining methods. Ore treatment process and its flowsheet are described.

entry.dc:title: ATHABASCA TAR SANDS.
entry.dc:creator: McConville L.
entry.dc:description: Monographic description of Athabasca tar sands begins with the official definition of tar sands as ″sand containing a highly viscous crude hydrocarbon material not recoverable in its natural state through a well by ordinary production methods″ . Paper is divided into several chapters discussing: geology and history of development of the deposit (proved reserves of crude bitumen in place are estimated to amount to about 900 multiplied by 10**9 bbls); commercialization of a deposit based on example of the Great Canadian Oil Sands, Ltd (GCOS) (present production of 55,000 bcpd of oil from 140,000 tpd of oil sands); existing and planned surface mining and refining projects (flowsheet of GCOS; plant is shown); recovery by in-situ methods; and future outlook.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING AND RECLAMATION, 3RD SYMPOSIUM, PAPERS, VOLUMES 1 AND 2, 1975.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Forty-one papers and four titles by various authors are presented. The topics discussed are: Federal coal leasing, pollutant discharge elimination, environment, surface mining, reclamation, revegetation, arid zone hydrology, coal mine spoils, preplanning, overburden materials, ecology, sulfur forms, watersheds, water chemistry, groundwater quality, photogrammetry and computer applications, drills, revegetation equipment, rehabilitation base-line data, sediment erosion control, soil losses, reclamation costs, economic system analysis, horizontal haul method, soil conservation plant materials, fertilizers lime, and mulch, forage grasses, noise, soil development, and land reclamation. Individual papers are indexed separately.

entry.dc:title: RESEARCH AND APPLIED TECHNOLOGY SYMPOSIUM ON MINED-LAND RECLAMATION, 2ND, PAPERS, 1974.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Twenty-five papers by various authors are presented. The topics discussed are: Mining and reclamation, controlled placement, surface and strip mining, revegetation, coal-leasing, federal and state permitting, ecology and restoration, mineral resource development, social and economic impacts of coal mining, sediment yield, hydrologic study of surface mined areas, groundwater quality, overburden properties, soil reconstruction, hydroseeding, pine breeding on acid spoil, all-season seeding, revegetation, surface mining technology, British reclamation experience and coal-mined land reclamation in Poland. Individual papers are indexed separately.

entry.dc:title: STATE-OF-THE-ART: SAND AND GRAVEL INDUSTRY.
entry.dc:creator: Newport B.
entry.dc:description: This report presents an overview of the sand and gravel industry in the United States and its relationship to the environment. The fate and effects of sediment generated by this surface mining activity on the benthic, planktonic, and fish communities of our waterways are discussed in detail. Problems of the sand and gravel industry, types of operations, status of current treatment technology, and legislation affecting the industry are reviewed.

entry.dc:title: EUBOEAN MAGNESITE MINING AND DEADBURNING IN GREECE.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Surface mining and deadburning (calcining) operations of the Scalistiri Group that are located on the island of Euboea, north of Athens and which produce 200,000 tonnes/year of MgO are described. Flowsheet of the magnesite ore treatment plant is shown.

entry.dc:title: WEIPA BAUXITE.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Australia has now become the world's largest producer of bauxite, and total production is still rising. Only 20 years ago, the country'S output was virtually negligible. Much of this rapid progress can be attributed to the high-grade discoveries at Weipa, in the Cape York peninsula area, the site of what is already the world's greatest single bauxite producer, with further excellent prospects for increases in production. Weipa has also proved to be the cornerstone for the very rapid development of a substantial proportion of Australia's own domestic aluminum industry. Geology of the orebody estimated to contain 520-million tons grading between 52 and 60% Al//2O//3 that cover a 73 sq mi area and of further 230 sq mi areas estimated to contain some 1,700-million tons of bauxite with grades of between 45 and 58% Al//2O//3 is described. Surface mining operations are removing an average 3 ft of overburden and are using wheel mounted, diesel operated, front end loaders that deliver straight to the haul trucks. Grade control, beneficiation, calcining plants, as well as railway and port facilities are described.

entry.dc:title: STEERING SYSTEMS FOR OFF-HIGHWAY TRUCKS.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Article describes the factors involved in the design of steering systems for the large-capacity motor trucks, around 200 tons, that are now in use in surface mining.

entry.dc:title: MINERALIZATION MODELS FOR MINE PLANNING AND EVALUATION.
entry.dc:creator: Perry J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Int Symp on the Appl of Comput and Math in the Miner Ind 12th Annu Proc Pap Colo Sch of Mines Golden Sect H
entry.dc:description: In order to evaluate a mineral deposit, a three dimensional model of the distribution of mineral values is required. For Surface Mining Systems this generally necessitates a regular block model with suitably chosen block size, bench interval and datum. This paper describes the sequential development of computerised methods for constructing such models from drill hole data for three stratiform deposits, each requiring different treatment. The methods have been developed at Roan Consolidated Mines Limited, in Zambia to deal with particular deposits encountered. In each case geological, mining and data processing staff have been involved in design and control.
